name: Agenesis of the corpus callosum
aliases: partial agenesis of the corpus callosum

reference.source: Volpe's Neurology of the Newborn / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Complete or partial absence of the corpus callosum, the major commissure connecting the cerebral hemispheres, and one of the most common brain malformations
It may be isolated or, more often clinically significant, part of a wider syndrome, chromosomal disorder, or metabolic condition, so a careful search for associated anomalies is essential
Characteristic MRI features include widely spaced parallel lateral ventricles, colpocephaly (dilated occipital horns), a high-riding third ventricle, and radiating medial gyri (the sunburst sign)
When complete agenesis is present, longitudinal Probst bundles run anteroposteriorly along the medial ventricular walls instead of crossing the midline
Outcome depends heavily on associated malformations and the underlying cause; truly isolated agenesis may be compatible with near-normal development

Clinical manifestations when present include developmental delay, epilepsy, and subtle deficits in interhemispheric transfer, and some syndromes such as Aicardi syndrome combine it with distinctive eye and seizure features
Diagnosis is by prenatal ultrasound and foetal or postnatal MRI, supplemented by genetic and metabolic testing to identify a cause
reference.pathophysiology: The corpus callosum forms in the first half of gestation as axons from cortical neurons cross the midline, guided by midline glial structures and molecular cues. Agenesis results when these guidance mechanisms fail, so callosal axons cannot cross and instead run longitudinally as Probst bundles along the medial ventricular walls. The malformation can arise from single-gene disorders, chromosomal imbalances, metabolic diseases, or disruptions of midline development, and it frequently coexists with other cerebral and systemic anomalies that determine the clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary callosal thinning from destructive or hypoxic-ischaemic injury
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to confirm complete or partial agenesis and detect associated malformations
Prenatal ultrasound and foetal MRI when suspected antenatally
Chromosomal microarray and, where indicated, exome sequencing
Metabolic screening for disorders that include callosal agenesis such as certain organic acidaemias
Ophthalmological examination, particularly to evaluate for Aicardi syndrome
Developmental assessment and electroencephalography if seizures occur
redFlags: Seizures, including infantile spasms, especially in the context of Aicardi syndrome
Features suggesting an underlying metabolic disorder such as decompensation or regression
Multiple associated malformations pointing to a syndromic or chromosomal cause
Progressive macrocephaly from an associated interhemispheric cyst or hydrocephalus
reference.prognosis: Isolated agenesis of the corpus callosum can be compatible with normal or near-normal neurodevelopment, though subtle cognitive and social deficits may emerge. When it is part of a syndromic, chromosomal, or metabolic disorder, the prognosis is dictated by the associated condition.
pitfalls: Labelling the malformation isolated without thorough imaging, genetic, and metabolic evaluation for associated conditions
Failing to consider Aicardi syndrome in a girl with callosal agenesis, seizures, and chorioretinal lacunae
Giving overly pessimistic prognosis for truly isolated cases
Confusing an associated interhemispheric cyst or colpocephaly with hydrocephalus requiring shunting
references: GeneReviews: Disorders of the Corpus Callosum
management: Determine and manage the underlying cause and any associated malformations, since these dictate prognosis and treatment
Treat epilepsy with antiseizure medication tailored to seizure type, including infantile spasms where present
Provide early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy for developmental delay
Screen for and manage associated anomalies through imaging, ophthalmological and metabolic assessment, including for Aicardi syndrome
Provide educational support and psychological input for cognitive, social and interhemispheric-transfer difficulties
Offer genetic counselling with chromosomal microarray and exome sequencing to define recurrence risk
Coordinate multidisciplinary follow-up through paediatric neurology, clinical genetics and allied health
